To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“A symmetry-driven accumulation of local features is a robust strategy for human re-identification”.

a) a symmetry-driven segmentation of the human body is a good way to extract local features, b) an accumulation of these local features is a good way of building a robust descriptor, c) the descriptor is robust enough to be used in a re-id procedure cast as an instance retrieval problem, which is d) suitable for multi-person tracking

1) symmetry is a good proxy to segment the human body into meaningful body parts,  and 2) the accumulation of features from local descriptors is a good strategy to improve re-id performance, especially in challenging scenarios.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of a descriptor that is invariant to pose, illumination and scale, and can be easily embedded in the context of a multi-person tracking system.

the development of a novel approach for person re-identification, which is able to cope with the challenging problems of occlusion, pose and illumination changes, and which can be easily integrated into a multi-target tracking scenario.
the design and implementation of an appearance model for re-id.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SDALF is a very good descriptor, which can be used to solve the re-id problem, but it is not the best descriptor in the world.

the proposed approach is a novel method to perform person re-identification, which is robust, fast, and effective, and that it is able to outperform the state of the arts on the most challenging public datasets.
our proposal outperforms the state of the-art in person re-identification by a significant margin, with an improvement of 10% on the standard benchmarking protocol.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a new descriptor that is robust to pose, scale, occlusions and illumination variations, and that can be easily integrated into a multi-person tracker.
we present an approach to model human appearance with the symmetry-driven accumulation of local features, which can be used as an observation model in a tracking-by-detection framework.
we present a novel method to model the appearance of humans in video sequences.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, by exploiting the symmetry of human appearance, we can obtain a very discriminant descriptor, that is able to cope with the appearance variations that are common in video surveillance scenarios, such as pose, scale, illumination, and occlusions.

, despite its simplicity, the proposed approach is able to achieve state-of-the-art results in the challenging VIPeR dataset, while outperforming the most recent approaches on the i-LIDS and PRID2011 datasets, which are more challenging in terms of number of persons and images per person.

, even though the state-of-the-art is already quite mature, there is still room for improvement in the field of person re-id, and we hope our contribution can help to push the state-of-the art further.
